frase_gancho.texto: A stone drum where a king grips fifteen peoples by the hair.

puente_narrativo.texto: Conquered peoples paid in tribute and in prisoners. Now look for a sibling of this cylinder, with eleven scenes of conquest, which turned up in 1988 beneath the streets of the city center.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before the Stone of Tízoc, a great cylinder almost one meter high and more than two and a half meters in diameter. It was commissioned by the tlatoani Tízoc, who ruled from 1481 to 1486. Walk around it: there are fifteen nearly identical scenes. In each one, the king, dressed in the regalia of a god, grips a defeated chief by the hair, and beside the captive a small glyph names the conquered people. It is a list of conquests set in stone. On top, the flat face has a sun disk with a hollow at the center and a channel running to the edge, designed to receive offerings. That is why the Mexica regarded it as a sacred monument, and not only a political one.

guion_largo.texto:
This stone has no spectacular face and no legend of terror, and that is why many people walk right past it. That is a mistake, because it is a document. The [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol), which you will see at the end of the hall, speaks of time; this one speaks of power: who was in command, whom he had defeated, and how he wanted to be remembered.

Notice the repetition. In all fifteen scenes, the king appears on the left, wearing either the hummingbird helmet of Huitzilopochtli or the regalia of Xiuhtecuhtli, the god of fire. On the right is an enemy chief, whom he grips by the hair. Seizing someone by the hair was the gesture of total victory, and you will find it in many codices. Each defeated chief has beside him the glyph of his people; one of them is Matlatzinco, in the Toluca valley. Fifteen names, fifteen defeats: a political map carved in stone.

But be careful: not everything a stone says is true. Tízoc reigned for barely five years, between his brother Axayácatl and his other brother Ahuízotl, and several historians believe his campaigns were more modest than what is shown here. What the monument shows is not what happened, but what power wanted people to believe. Today governments use speeches and advertisements; the Mexica used basalt.

Behind that list stands a very young empire. Just half a century earlier, in 1428, the Mexica had rebelled against Azcapotzalco, to which they paid tribute, together with the Texcocans of Nezahualcóyotl and with Tlacopan. That Triple Alliance became the most powerful force in central Mexico, and stones like this one were its way of reminding everyone who was in command now.

It also had a ritual use. The Mexica called this type of stone temalácatl and cuauhxicalli, a sacred vessel for offerings. According to the chronicles of the friars, during the festival of Tlacaxipehualiztli, dedicated to [Xipe Tótec](mna_s04_xipe_totec), a high-ranking war captive was tied by the waist to a circular stone. He was given a club decorated with feathers, and he had to fight Mexica warriors armed with real weapons. Afterward he was sacrificed. Specialists debate whether this stone was used in exactly that way, but its shape fits that description very well.

If you lean over and look at the top, you will see the sun disk and the central hollow, joined to a channel. It is thought that the blood of the offerings was poured there, to feed the Sun. Some think the hollow and the channel were added after the scenes were carved, which suggests that the stone may have changed its function over time.

Its modern history holds a curious coincidence. It was found on December 17, 1791, during drainage works in the Plaza de Armas, what is today the Zócalo. Exactly one year earlier, in that same plaza, the Sun Stone had been found. Two giant discoveries, one year apart. The story goes that some stonecutters were about to break it up to make paving stones, and that some scholars stopped them. In time, it ended up in the old National Museum.

When you walk around it, think of both meanings at once: a picture of victory and an offering table. For the Mexica they were not opposites. Winning a war was also a way of obtaining what the Sun needed to keep on walking.

texto: Count the fifteen scenes and find the king’s hand in the defeated chief’s hair
Find the small glyph beside each captive: it is the name of his people
Lean over and look at the top: can you see the hollow in the center and the channel?

texto.Dimensions: 94 cm high x 265 cm in diameter

texto.pregunta: Myth: Tízoc was the greatest Mexica conqueror, and that is why his stone shows him defeating fifteen peoples.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Tízoc reigned for only about five years, and several historians believe his campaigns were modest. The stone does not tell what happened, but how power wanted it to be remembered.
